title: Quantum oscillation spectroscopy of Fermi-surface topologies in tetralayer graphene
authors: Abhijit Halder, Harsh Varshney, Snehamoyee Hazra, Santu Kumar Bera, Souvik Chakraborty, Ujjal Roy, Takashi Taniguchi, Kenji Watanabe, Amit Agarwal, Anindya Das
abstract: Quantum oscillations offer a direct probe of Fermi-surface topology and electronic degeneracy, yet disentangling both simultaneously across the Lifshitz transitions of multiband systems has remained an open experimental challenge. Here, we use Shubnikov-de Haas spectroscopy on a high-mobility, dual-gated Bernal-stacked tetralayer graphene (B-4LG) device to quantitatively reconstruct the complete sequence of six distinct Fermi-surface topologies-gully, annular, singly connected, and multiband pockets. The extracted oscillation frequencies determine the extremal momentum-space areas and their spin, valley, and gully-resolved degeneracies, in quantitative agreement with our tight-binding calculations. We further show that a perpendicular magnetic-field, combined with displacement-field lifts the valley degeneracy through an orbital-Zeeman coupling, producing a single-particle valley splitting of several $meV$, far larger than in bilayer or trilayer graphene. Our work demonstrates a framework for tracking Fermi-surface topologies and their flavor degeneracies in multiband quantum materials.
summary: This research uses Shubnikov-de Haas spectroscopy on tetralayer graphene to quantitatively map out six distinct Fermi-surface topologies and their degeneracies. By combining magnetic and electric fields, the authors demonstrate a novel method to lift the valley degeneracy, providing a powerful tool for characterizing multiband quantum materials.
main_problem: The primary challenge is quantitatively reconstructing both the topology of Fermi pockets and their associated flavor degeneracies across Lifshitz transitions in multiband quantum systems.
main_result: The study successfully mapped six distinct Fermi-surface topologies in tetralayer graphene and demonstrated that combining a perpendicular magnetic field with an electric displacement field can lift the valley degeneracy via orbital-Zeeman coupling.
method: Shubnikov-de Haas (SdH) spectroscopy is used to probe extremal areas, while tight-binding models are employed for theoretical comparison of degeneracies and splitting mechanisms.
model_or_system: The physical system is a high-mobility, dual-gated Bernal-stacked tetralayer graphene (B-4LG) device. The electronic structure is modeled using an extended tight-binding Hamiltonian incorporating interlayer hopping and external fields.
key_observables: Fermi-surface topologies (gully, annular, etc.), oscillation frequencies ($f_i$), spin/valley degeneracies ($g_i$), and the valley splitting energy ($\Delta E_{	ext{valley}}$).
important_parameters: Carrier density ($n$), perpendicular magnetic field ($B_\perp$), and displacement field ($D/\epsilon_0$). The splitting can reach several meV.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the applicability of the Lifshitz–Kosevich formalism for SdH oscillations, and theoretical calculations use specific tight-binding approximations.
figures_summary: Figures show the evolution of six Fermi-surface topologies (Fig. 1), transport signatures confirming these regimes (Fig. 2), quantitative mapping of outer/inner contour frequencies vs. density (Fig. 3), and calculated single-particle Landau level spectra demonstrating valley splitting (Fig. 4, Fig. 6).
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the experimental challenge using SdH spectroscopy on B-4LG to map topological transitions across six regimes. It then details how tuning fields ($D$ and $B$) allows for quantitative reconstruction of degeneracies. Finally, it uses advanced tight-binding calculations to theoretically explain the large valley splitting observed.
why_interesting: The work provides a concrete experimental framework using quantum oscillations to map complex electronic band structures (topology) while simultaneously quantifying subtle symmetry breaking effects like valley splitting, which is crucial for understanding topological quantum materials.
